title: Shale-oil recovery from the matrix

concept.text: The proposed innovation is sustained recovery of substantially more oil from the extremely low-permeability rock matrix of a developed shale-oil reservoir. Hydraulic and natural fractures provide pathways toward wells, but oil must first move through the surrounding rock to reach them. The central advance would combine effective fracture access with enough matrix-to-fracture transport to raise total recovery across a multi-well area. The 2023 SPE grand-challenge article identifies low recovery, ultra-low permeability and difficult matrix transport as the underlying engineering problem.

Proposed scope: demonstrate roughly 20–40% total lifetime recovery of the original oil in place within a defined developed shale-oil area, against a documented single-digit primary-recovery baseline. The improvement would need evidence of drainage beyond the volume immediately accessible to existing fractures. This is a proposed capability and target, not an established recovery standard or an achievement demonstrated in the supplied record. The concept leaves the successful method open: it could involve injectants, thermal methods, fracture management or a combination.

significance.text: Horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing enabled extraction from unconventional shale resources, yet the July 2023 SPE article reports that existing shale-oil wells decline rapidly and ultimate recoveries are often below 10%. A method that substantially improves matrix drainage would address a limitation that additional access through fractures alone does not necessarily resolve. That last point is an engineering inference from the article’s separate emphasis on necessary fractures and difficult matrix transport.

For a fixed original oil-in-place volume, higher recovery efficiency directly means more cumulative recovered oil. Illustratively, increasing total recovery from 5% to 20–40% would yield four to eight times as much oil from that same denominator. This arithmetic is conditional on achieving the proposed recovery, and the illustrative 5% baseline is not a measured value for a particular development. The EIA/ARI methodology defines recovery efficiency as recovered oil divided by oil in place.

Conditional downstream significance: if the method transferred across reservoir settings and could be deployed economically, existing developed shale provinces could yield substantially more cumulative oil. Success on one pad would establish a local capability; broader impact would depend on geology, fluid properties, fracture systems, operating requirements and deployment. Neither commercial feasibility nor province-wide performance is demonstrated here. The supplied evidence also does not quantify tight oil’s share of U.S. crude supply.

The comparison with conventional-oil recovery is useful as an ambition to recover a much larger fraction of oil in place, but it has limits. The documented shale challenge emphasizes nanodarcy-scale permeability and slow matrix transport. It does not establish that capillarity or preferential flow cease to matter in shale, or that all conventional reservoirs share one recovery mechanism. The proposed 20–40% target should therefore stand on its own; its description as a historical conventional-field recovery band is not substantiated by the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is field-scale, sustained transfer of enough oil from the matrix into producing fractures to produce a large increase in total recovery. The 2023 SPE article reports permeabilities often on the order of nanodarcies, extremely low flow rates and transport dominated by diffusion. It also identifies geomechanics and rock compaction as important. A successful process must work within those coupled transport and mechanical constraints over a useful operating period.

Delivering a recovery agent through the reservoir is itself a barrier. The SPE article says low permeability hampers well-to-well recovery methods and identifies understanding injectant transport in the matrix and interaction with fractures as challenges. Single-well huff-and-puff—alternating injection, a soak period and production—offers one operating approach, but using that approach does not by itself demonstrate broad matrix drainage or a large lifetime recovery increase.

Mechanistic questions retained from the research include whether gas slip and Knudsen diffusion materially affect a particular recovery process, and how adsorption and confinement influence oil in organic pores. The supplied review could not verify these additions: neither cited gas-flow paper has retained source text, and the oil adsorption/confinement claim lacks inspected supporting evidence. These remain possible considerations rather than established explanations for this innovation. Nanometer-scale pore width alone should not be presented here as a universal threshold for failure of Darcy flow; gas-flow mechanisms also cannot substitute for evidence about liquid-oil recovery.

Proposed engineering requirement: connect pore- and core-scale understanding to predictive pad-scale performance, including the amount of matrix contacted, the time required to release oil and the resulting cumulative recovery. An apparent-permeability correction or a model that matches production could be useful, but neither alone would establish the sought recovery capability. Attribution would need to distinguish newly accessed matrix oil from accelerated production, fracture-held fluids or redistribution among connected wells.

current_state.text: The 2013 EIA/ARI methodology reports estimated recovery efficiencies for 28 U.S. tight-oil plays ranging from about 1% to 9%, with an unweighted average near 3.5%. These values were derived from calculated oil in place and type-curve recovery calculations. They are assessment estimates, not completed-lifetime measurements of every field, and the population includes tight sand and limestone settings as well as shale. The unweighted average is not a production-weighted national recovery factor or a present-day universal shale-oil baseline.

The SPE grand-challenge article published on 1 July 2023 reports shale-oil ultimate recoveries often below 10%, describes the low-permeability and diffusion-dominated transport challenge, and identifies single-well huff-and-puff as the most common improved-recovery method. It discusses gases, chemicals and thermal methods as recovery approaches. This documents the challenge and approaches discussed at that time; it supplies no demonstration of the proposed 20–40% pad-scale endpoint.

The research also cites the 2009 paper “Nanopores and Apparent Permeability of Gas Flow in Mudrocks (Shales and Siltstone)” and the 2021 review “Gas Flow Models of Shale.” Neither source has retained text in the supplied source index. Their reported abstract-level descriptions therefore remain unverified within this review record. Claims that apparent-permeability models fit shale-gas rates, or operate as corrections within a Darcy-shaped equation, cannot be assessed from the retained evidence. This access limitation does not establish that those claims are false. In any event, these are gas-flow references, not measurements of shale-oil recovery.

The supplied review reports complete retained text for the relevant SPE article and the 27-page EIA/ARI methodology, sufficient for the textual findings above. Linked SPE tables and figures were not visually inspected. No bounded freshness-search entries were supplied for later developments, so these historical sources do not establish whether the proposed capability remained unachieved on 1 November 2026. The record supports dated motivation and numerical estimates, while leaving the contemporary frontier unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed principal demonstration: within one clearly bounded developed shale-oil area, achieve roughly 20–40% total lifetime recovery of original oil in place across a multi-well pad, against a documented single-digit primary-recovery baseline. Define the reservoir volume, oil-in-place denominator, included wells and accounting period before evaluating performance, and report uncertainty in both oil in place and recovered oil. The numerical target is a proposal, not an established industry standard.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-well pad achieves roughly 20–40% lifetime recovery against single-digit baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution requirement: use converging measurements and reservoir analysis to show that the gain includes drainage of matrix beyond the volume readily accessible to existing fractures. Account for interwell communication and distinguish a higher ultimate recovery from merely faster production. Report total recovery, absolute percentage-point improvement and relative improvement separately. For example, moving from 5% to 7% recovery is a two-percentage-point increase and a 40% relative increase; it remains below the proposed endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Recovery gains include matrix drainage beyond existing fractures’ accessible volume

completion_criteria.text: Proposed duration and reproducibility requirements: sustain the gain through the pad’s operating life and reproduce the result in additional wells or pads with sufficiently documented geology, operating conditions and recovery accounting. If lifetime recovery is projected before operations are complete, separate observed cumulative production from the forecast tail, disclose the assumptions and test forecasts prospectively as production continues. A short huff-and-puff pilot with a small incremental gain would provide useful partial evidence but would not complete this demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Lifetime recovery gains reproduce in additional wells or pads

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report injectant consumption and recycling, energy and water requirements, operating costs, environmental effects and relevant reservoir or well constraints alongside recovered oil. The SPE article explicitly frames improved recovery as a goal to pursue with minimal environmental impact; the supplied record establishes no numerical acceptance limits for these factors. A convincing result should identify where the method works and where it fails. Finite demonstrations establish breadth across tested conditions, not universal applicability to shale provinces.
completion_criteria.label: Recovery reporting covers resource costs, environmental effects and applicability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PET-01, “Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow,” overlaps through the need to predict matrix-to-fracture transport and recovery before observing the outcome. Its endpoint is predictive capability; PET-05’s endpoint is materially greater recovered oil. PET-08, “Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume,” could help constrain oil-in-place estimates and demonstrate where drainage occurred. Measurement capability would support PET-05 without itself releasing the oil.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-02, “Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors,” shares the ambition of raising recovered fractions. PET-05 specifically addresses shale matrix transport under ultra-low permeability. The supplied PET-02 title does not establish its detailed mechanisms or target values, so the earlier categorical distinction between conventional capillarity/channeling and shale transport cannot be retained. The entries remain distinct without assuming their mechanisms never overlap.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-04, “Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen,” concerns converting kerogen into producible hydrocarbons, whereas PET-05 concerns recovering oil already present in the reservoir. PET-09, “Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature,” emphasizes mobility of bitumen; PET-11, “In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude,” emphasizes changing bitumen into a product meeting a specification. All may involve transport or fluid-property changes, but neither bitumen mobility nor hydrocarbon conversion establishes shale-oil matrix recovery.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-03, “Commercial gas production from methane hydrate,” and PET-06, “Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground,” also concern obtaining useful products from subsurface resources. Their respective endpoints involve hydrate gas production and hydrogen production with underground retention of other products. PET-05 instead seeks a higher recovered fraction of reservoir oil. Only titles were supplied for these entries, so more detailed mechanistic overlap remains undetermined.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-07, “Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty,” could affect access and development costs, but constructing a well does not establish improved matrix drainage. PET-10, “A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound,” could become relevant to an injection-based PET-05 process through pressure management and seismic constraints. Its endpoint is a tested pressure-plan bound, distinct from the oil-recovery endpoint. These relationships are inferred from the roster titles rather than supporting technical dossiers.

change_log.change: Preserved PET-05’s identity and developed its central capability as sustained matrix-to-fracture oil recovery across a developed multi-well area.
change_log.reason: The review supports the underlying recovery challenge; limitations in ancillary mechanism claims do not invalidate the concept.

change_log.change: Corrected the 2013 recovery figures to estimated efficiencies for 28 U.S. tight-oil plays, including tight sand and limestone settings, derived from oil-in-place and type-curve calculations.
change_log.reason: The original wording risked presenting assessment estimates as universal observed shale-oil lifetime recovery.

change_log.change: Retained the 1–9% range and approximately 3.5% unweighted average while separating them from the 2023 SPE description and any present-day baseline.
change_log.reason: The quantitative result is supported, but its date, population and weighting limit its interpretation.

change_log.change: Clarified the proposed 20–40% endpoint as total lifetime recovery of original oil in place and removed its asserted standing as a conventional-field benchmark.
change_log.reason: The target is a coherent proposal; the supplied evidence does not substantiate the historical benchmark characterization.

change_log.change: Integrated injectant transport, fracture interaction, geomechanics, compaction and thermal approaches into the technical explanation.
change_log.reason: These useful details from the review explain the engineering challenge more fully than the original emphasis on fractures and gas-flow corrections.

change_log.change: Recast gas slip, Knudsen diffusion, oil adsorption and confinement as unverified mechanistic considerations and removed the categorical pore-width threshold for Darcy-law failure.
change_log.reason: The gas papers lack retained text, pore width alone does not establish a universal threshold in this record, and oil-specific mechanisms lack inspected support.

change_log.change: Separated gas-flow modeling claims from oil-recovery achievements and preserved the source-access limitation.
change_log.reason: Gas modeling is not evidence of increased shale-oil recovery, and missing text prevents assessment without proving the cited claims false.

change_log.change: Made production multiplication explicitly conditional and local, with transferability and deployment required for province-wide impact.
change_log.reason: Higher recovery directly increases recovered volume for a fixed denominator, but one-area success does not establish commercial or geographic generality.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical PET-02 mechanism comparison with a qualified distinction and added relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Only roster titles were supplied; they support careful conceptual comparisons without merging entries or inventing their technical specifications.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to cover attribution, uncertainty, observed versus forecast recovery, reproducibility and practical operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These distinguish a convincing recovery demonstration from a short production response, optimistic forecast or ambiguous percentage gain.

change_log.change: Excluded the unrelated IPCC and Nevada PDFs from supporting evidence and retained the lack of a contemporary freshness assessment.
change_log.reason: Those PDFs are not copies of the petroleum article, and retrieval dates do not establish the November 2026 research frontier.

unresolved_issues: No supplied freshness-search record establishes developments after the historical sources or whether the proposed capability remained unachieved on 1 November 2026.
Neither gas-flow paper has retained text, leaving its specific flow-regime and apparent-permeability modeling claims unassessed.
The relevance and magnitude of adsorption and confinement effects for oil recovery require oil-specific supporting evidence.

The 20–40% target’s feasibility, economic viability and transferability across shale settings are not established; its characterization as a historical conventional-field benchmark also remains unverified.
A demonstration still needs site-specific definitions of the original oil-in-place volume, primary-recovery baseline, drainage evidence and acceptable uncertainty.
Operational, economic and environmental acceptance limits remain to be defined; the supplied evidence provides no established numerical thresholds.
Detailed overlap with PET-02 and other roster concepts cannot be resolved from titles alone, and the historical calibration examples mentioned in the review were not supplied.

brief.title: More oil from rock around existing wells
possible: Oil producers could recover much more oil from shale, rock that lets oil move through it extremely slowly. Oil trapped in the rock between cracks could reach those cracks and flow toward existing wells.
The goal is sustained recovery across a group of wells sharing a developed area. Success would mean extracting a much larger share of the oil originally there over the wells’ working lives.
why: Shale wells lose production quickly while leaving much of their oil underground. Getting more of that oil out would increase the total supply recovered from an already developed area.
Moving oil through the surrounding rock would address a problem that opening cracks alone does not solve. Producers could gain more cumulative oil from the same underground resource.

sources.showed: They described rapid declines in shale-well production and lifetime recovery often below 10%. They identified extremely slow movement through the rock as a central obstacle.
sources.quote: However, production from existing shale oil wells declines quickly, and ultimate recoveries are often less than 10%.
sources.cited_for: Much of the oil remains underground, and moving it through the rock is a central challenge.
sources.not_established: The article does not demonstrate a sustained, large recovery increase across a group of wells.

sources.who: Advanced Resources International and the US Energy Information Administration
sources.showed: Their assessment estimated low recovery across US tight-oil formations, averaging about 3.5%. These were estimates, and the formations included rocks other than shale.
sources.cited_for: Resource assessments provide a low-recovery starting point for the proposed improvement.
sources.not_established: Assessment estimates do not establish completed lifetime recovery or a baseline for a particular demonstration site.

sources.showed: This is a review of models describing gas flow through shale.
sources.cited_for: It concerns how gas moves through shale.
sources.not_established: Gas-flow models do not demonstrate increased recovery of liquid oil.

sources.showed: This paper concerns gas flow through tiny pores in shale and siltstone.
sources.cited_for: It concerns how tiny pores affect gas flow through rock.
sources.not_established: Gas-flow behavior does not establish how much liquid oil a group of wells can recover.

shown: The SPE authors describe approaches using gases, chemicals and heat. The most common improved-recovery approach alternates injection, a waiting period and production in the same well. These approaches have not established the proposed recovery target across a group of wells.
missing: A field demonstration must sustain enough oil movement from the surrounding rock into cracks to produce a large total recovery gain.
Measurements must distinguish newly reached oil from faster production, oil already in cracks or oil shifted between connected wells.
Recovery gains must persist over the wells’ working lives and repeat elsewhere.

milestones.label: A group of wells reaches the lifetime recovery target
milestones.explanation: A defined developed area would have to recover roughly 20–40% of its original oil against a documented single-digit baseline, with uncertainty reported. This would establish the scale of the gain.

milestones.label: Extra oil comes from beyond readily reached rock
milestones.explanation: Measurements and analysis would have to trace extra oil to rock beyond what existing cracks readily reach. This would distinguish wider drainage from faster production or transfers between wells.

milestones.label: Lifetime gains repeat in additional wells or sites
milestones.explanation: Gains would have to last through operations and repeat in additional wells or sites, with forecasts separated from measured production and tested over time. This would establish durability and repeatability.

milestones.label: Resource use, environmental effects and operating limits are reported
milestones.explanation: Results would have to include injected-material use and recycling, energy, water, costs, environmental effects and operating limits. These would establish the conditions and burdens of achieving the gain.

uncertain: Whether the recovery target is physically achievable and economically viable across different shale settings remains open.
The effects of oil sticking to pore surfaces and being confined in tiny pores need oil-specific evidence.
Acceptable uncertainty in recovery estimates and acceptable resource costs and environmental effects remain to be defined.

page.title: Enhanced oil recovery from shale reservoirs
page.definition: A field process recovers at least 40% of a shale reservoir's original oil while at least doubling site recovery. It mobilizes oil in the matrix, the rock between fractures; recovery factor means recovered oil divided by original oil in place.

goal.need: EIA/ARI's 2013 assessment estimated recovery efficiencies of about 1–9%, averaging about 3.5%, across 28 U.S. tight-oil plays. These were type-curve estimates, including tight sandstone and limestone as well as shale. On 19 May 2026, NETL reported typical primary oil recovery of 3–10% from hydraulically fractured unconventional formations. Increasing recovery addresses the oil remaining after primary production.

figures.caption: Estimated oil recovery efficiency in 28 U.S. tight-oil plays, 2013.
figures.note: Oil recovered divided by oil in place; type-curve assessment estimates, not completed-lifetime measurements or a production-weighted national average.

statements.body: Society of Petroleum Engineers, January 2023 grand-challenges workshop
statements.quote: To meet global demand, we must improve recovery with minimal environmental impact.
statements.context: The workshop report identifies improved recovery from tight/shale resources as a technical grand challenge.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, National Energy Technology Laboratory
statements.quote: Our task involves finding safe and cost-effective strategies to recover far greater percentages of the oil and gas left behind in those reservoirs
statements.context: Angela Goodman, quoted on 19 May 2026, discussing shale and other tight reservoirs after primary recovery.

completion.title: Shale-oil field recovery reaches ≥40% and doubles the site's recovery factor.
completion.criterion: Field performance demonstrates ≥40% recovery of original oil in place over project life and ≥2 times current site recovery. Lifetime water-disposal volume and production cost per barrel of oil equivalent, including capital and operating costs, remain at or below site benchmarks. Estimated ultimate recovery specifies assumed well life.
completion.set_by: ARPA-E UNLOCK, DE-FOA-0003630, Section I.E.1, Table 1; thresholds are tabulated.
completion.basis: UNLOCK specifies field performance and accepts estimated ultimate recovery; it sets no separate matrix-drainage threshold.

milestones.title: Laboratory experiments validate a mechanism for recovering oil from shale rock.
milestones.criterion: Analytical and laboratory studies validate the recovery mechanism: DOE's technology readiness level 3, which sets no recovery-percentage cutoff. A report dated 17 November 2017 describes two Eagle Ford outcrop plugs tested with nitrogen at 1,000 psi: first-cycle recovery increased from 2% to 5.6% and from 1.8% to 4.8% as soaking increased from 0.25 to 48 hours. These are core-scale results.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Levels, TRL-3; generic definition applied to shale-oil recovery.
milestones.threshold_quote: Proof of concept validation has been achieved at this level.

milestones.title: Site-specific laboratory results validate shale-oil recovery capable of meeting UNLOCK's field targets.
milestones.criterion: Tests on site-specific core and fluids, supported by numerical models, validate the process's ability to meet field recovery, water-disposal and cost targets.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E UNLOCK, DE-FOA-0003630, Section I.D.2, laboratory-validation gate.
milestones.threshold_quote: laboratory experiments validate the technology’s ability to meet the targets

milestones.title: A shale-oil recovery process operates as an integrated pilot in a producing reservoir.
milestones.criterion: An at- or near-full-scale recovery process operates in a shale reservoir with supporting systems integrated and most functions available for demonstration and testing: DOE's TRL-7 integrated-pilot criterion. On 5 May 2016, EOG reported increased oil production from four Eagle Ford pilots involving 15 producing wells after more than three years of testing. This company result was not peer reviewed; it does not establish a formal TRL rating or 40% recovery of original oil in place.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Levels, TRL-7; generic definition applied to shale-oil recovery.
milestones.threshold_quote: System prototyping demonstration in operational environment.

not_found: No inspected field result established all of UNLOCK's recovery, water-disposal and cost targets.
No published quantitative acceptance test was found for attributing additional recovery specifically to matrix drainage.
No inspected result established UNLOCK's site-specific laboratory-validation gate.

results.finding: Nitrogen huff-n-puff tests on two Eagle Ford shale plugs achieved up to 5.6% first-cycle oil recovery.
results.detail: At 1,000 psi, first-cycle recovery increased with soaking time from 0.25 to 48 hours. These are core-scale laboratory results.
results.quote:
Applying soaking period from 0.25-hr to 48-hr, the RFs in cycle one raised from 2% to 5.6% for 
core LEF_1 and from 1.8% to 4.8% for core LEF_2.

results.finding: CO2 huff-n-puff recovered 14.1% of original oil in place from one shale core.
results.detail: NMR measurements showed oil mobilization from inorganic pores. The core was soaked at 11.0 MPa for three cycles; the study tested three cores in total.
results.quote:
It was found
that the cumulative oil recovery (COR) from total pores after three
cycles was merely 14.1% OOIP, among which the COR of the ﬁrst
cycle was 7.93% OOIP, accounting for more than half COR after three
cycles.

results.finding: Shale core CO2 huff-and-puff experiments, sample size not stated: best-case oil recovery reached 75% with surfactant.
results.detail: The report attributes improved recovery to surfactant-induced wettability alteration; the best case increased from 71% to 75%, while other surfactants had little or detrimental effect. The source does not state a sample size or establish peer review.
results.quote:
o Huff n’ puff experiments:  In the best case, oil recovery increase by a surfactant dissolved in CO2 was modest 
(e.g. 71% to 75%, by 0.1% of a branched tridecyl ethoxylate with 9 EO units), other surfactants had little effect or 
detrimental effect

results.finding: CO2 huff and puff on four Gulong shale cores achieved 21.84% average utilization efficiency.
results.detail: Site-specific core and crude-oil tests were supported by reservoir simulations. The results do not establish 40% recovery, a doubling of site recovery, or the water-disposal and cost targets.
results.quote: The average utilization efficiency was 21.67% for 4 rounds and 21.84% for 6 rounds.

results.finding: East Nesson EOR pilot injected one well; an estimated 8,400 barrels of incremental oil would be produced from two wells over five years.
results.detail: The pilot integrated gas, water and surfactant injection with production and surveillance. The report does not establish that the process was at or near full scale or that most functions were available for demonstration and testing. The oil volume is a decline-curve forecast.
results.quote:
Decline curve analyses conducted by the EERC and Liberty Resources indicate 
that approximately 8400 bbl of incremental oil will be produced as a result of the EOR test from 
two wells on the DSU, the Haley 10-MBH well and an offset well.

results.finding: CO2 huff-and-puff in one producing shale well increased daily oil production from 1.0 to 4.8 t.
results.detail: The field test demonstrates injection, soaking and subsequent production in a shale reservoir. The paper does not establish that supporting systems were integrated or that most functions of an at- or near-full-scale process were available for demonstration and testing.
results.quote:
The daily oil production steadily increased from 1.0 t 
before the CO 2 injection to 4.8 t, and then gradually de-
creased.

results.finding: Six Wolfcamp field core plugs yielded 42.64%–49.65% oil recovery after eight methane injection cycles.
results.detail: The cores and crude oil came from Apache's Lin field, and related numerical modeling is reported. The laboratory results do not validate field recovery, water-disposal and cost targets.
results.quote:
of the core plugs with diameter of 1’’, 1.5’’, 2’’, 3’ ’, 3.5’’ and 4’’ are 49.65%, 48.57%, 47.76%, 
46.15%, 43.55% and 42.64%, respectively.

results.finding: CO2 huff-n-puff recovered 30.19% of original oil in place from one shale core after three cycles.
results.detail: The study used outcrop cores and degassed oil, omitted connate water and numerical modeling, and did not validate field recovery, water-disposal, or cost targets.
results.quote:
exceeding MMP, the COR after three cycles achieved 30.19% OOIP,
while the oil recovery of IPs reached 70.04% OOIP

results.finding: A shale-oil-CO2 contact-angle test showed a 71° increase with surfactant; sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The test supports wettability alteration but does not establish site-specific recovery, numerical-model validation, water-disposal performance, or field costs.

results.finding: Four Gulong shale cores reached 21.84% average utilization efficiency after six CO₂ huff-and-puff rounds.
results.detail: NMR measurements characterized oil drainage from different pore sizes. The authors attribute improved drainage to oil expansion and reduced viscosity from dissolved CO₂.
results.quote: The average utilization efficiency was 21.67% for 4 rounds and 21.84% for 6 rounds.

results.finding: CO2 huff-n-puff tests on 3 Jiyang shale cores produced 40.19% of oil in the Scheme 2 core after four cycles.
results.detail: NMR observations support diffusion and mass transfer as mechanisms for mobilizing oil. Cores were saturated with n-dodecane.

results.finding: In tests on 3 Jiyang shale cores, the Scheme 2 core reached 40.19% oil production after four cycles.
results.detail: The tests used n-dodecane rather than identified site-specific reservoir fluids. The laboratory and modeling results do not validate the field recovery, water-disposal and cost targets together.

results.finding: Gas huff-n-puff tests on two Haynesville shale cores recovered 48% additional oil from the live-oil core.
results.detail: Seven cycles were performed on each core. Pressure and recovery profiles support gas penetration and expansion as mechanisms; the authors note that differences between cores may affect the comparison.
results.quote: 48% of additional oil recovery was observed
